bajkaj-landfill-land-taken-before-paymen.community: The landfill at Bajkaj-Palavli needed 3.23 hectares of land. The land acquisition completion report of October 2014 says that covered 21 plots belonging to 20 owners, that the land was used for livestock grazing, and that there were no houses or other structures on it. Its Table 1, headed as per the resettlement plan, names every owner with the size of the plot and the area taken, and a second table repeats the same totals with the number of plots corrected. Four plots were taken in full: Sinan Kuci 892 square metres, Ago Kuci 1,859, Nedin Kuci 2,349 and Shahin Haderi 7,123. In total 32,320 square metres were taken out of 54,235. The report says the land should have been acquired before construction started and was not: "the contractor accessed the land before compensations were paid, which caused tensions, consequently work stoppages at the landfill site from November 2013 to February 2014." It also says the delay came from administrative requirements, including the duty on owners to produce full proof of title, and that the number of plots and the land area first recorded did not match the final figures, so the Council of Ministers had to amend its expropriation decision. Payments were made in early February 2014 after that amendment and the works resumed in mid-February. Total compensation was estimated at 19,547,136 lek, about US$193,920; the report's payment table, dated as of January 2015, lists 15,055,387 lek paid. As of October 2014, 13 of the 20 owners had been paid in full. The report gives two accounts of the remaining seven in the same document: the executive summary says they are "either deceased or living abroad, mostly in Greece", and section 3.2 says seven owners "have not applied for compensation", with migration the reason for three and the death of the proprietor for four. The money for those cases was placed in an escrow account and the report says one family was finalising an inheritance procedure to become eligible. Two further owners were identified as affected by the access road. The report's own monitoring table says the affected people were not dependent on the land, so their incomes were not adversely affected, and that there were no new complaints or community opposition. Three commitments to the villages were recorded as finished in 2014: the road from Bajkaj to Palavli, the two village squares and their entrance roads, and an upgrade of the water supply.
bajkaj-landfill-land-taken-before-paymen.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 103 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The landfill documents count 20 land owners and 21 plots and record no houses on the land. The Bank's completion report says the waste transfer station at Himara, the project's other waste site, involved no economic or physical displacement.
bajkaj-landfill-land-taken-before-paymen.killed_note: No death is recorded in the completion report or in the land acquisition completion report.
bajkaj-landfill-land-taken-before-paymen.outcome: The Bank's completion report of 27 April 2016 says that at project closure in March 2015 there were no outstanding social safeguards issues and that the compensation question "was resolved before the project closure date". Its safeguards annex gives different numbers from the borrower's report: it says the acquisition took 3.2 hectares "from 21 project-affected people", that full payments were made in 13 cases, and that in 8 cases the people were deceased or living abroad. The borrower's report of October 2014 gives 20 owners, 13 paid and 7 outstanding. The same annex says a resettlement plan for the landfill construction "was prepared and implemented in compliance with World Bank operational policy (OP 4.12)", and that there had been no new complaints or community opposition to the landfill since April 2014. The landfill was 90 per cent built in October 2014 and the works were completed. The report's payment table lists 13 plots paid and 8 unpaid; two of the unpaid plots carry the same owner's name.

fields_add.community: The Bank's own completion report, dated 27 April 2016, sets out the case under project number P086807, credit agreement C4083-AL. It says the Executive Directors authorised the Panel investigation on 1 November 2007 and that the residents of Jale filed several complaints. The requesters said the Construction Police of the Municipality of Vlora had demolished their permanent residences in whole or in part, that the police singled out Jale while sparing other similar buildings along the coast because public officials wanted to clear space for a resort at and around the site, and that the Bank had failed to supervise the work it was financing.
fields_add.outcome: Bank management told the Board there was no direct or indirect link between the project and the demolitions, and said they were part of a government programme that had started in 2001. The Panel concluded that the decision not to apply the resettlement policy at appraisal and during implementation was a root cause in the mishandling of the demolitions. Management then acknowledged "serious errors in project preparation and supervision, along with errors in communication with the Board of the World Bank". It agreed to pay the requesters' legal costs for a case-by-case legal review of the April 2007 demolitions, to appoint an independent observer to monitor that review, and to apply assistance packages retroactively to poor and vulnerable people affected by the demolitions. A footnote was added to the Bank's resettlement policy stating that the policy does not apply to land use planning activities unless they involve Bank-assisted investments that require the taking of land. The completion report of April 2016 says the project had disbursed only about 25 per cent before the investigation, that the suspension of disbursements lasted 17 months and was lifted in June 2010, and that the project closed on 31 March 2015.

bilotserkivka-m03-bypass-house-damage.community: The project rebuilt part of the M-03 Kyiv-Kharkiv-Dovzhanskyi road and built three bypasses in Poltava oblast: Pokrovska Bahachka, Krasnohorivka and the first stage of the Poltava bypass. The addendum of 9 December 2017 records a house damaged by the works. It says: "No physical resettlement was induced at any stage of the acquisition. However, one PAP in Krasnogorivka bypass has now approached the local administration for resettlement through replacement of house in the same village (Bilotserkivka) as the walls of the house developed cracks due to ongoing road construction works in the RoW about 10 meters away from the house." The same paragraph says the case "was reviewed, found deserving, and is being considered eligible for relocation and resettlement assistance" under the original plan's entitlement matrix, and that the person was added to the list of affected people because the approved plan had not identified them. Addendum No.2, dated December 2018 on its cover, records an acquisition at the same village for a different reason. It says a design change made after residents and local authorities asked for two cattle passes and local roads so people could move around the village without using the main road "resulted in need for additional acquisition of 3 land plots, 1 house and involuntary resettlement of 1 person in the Bilotserkivka village". It does not mention the cracked walls, and no document says the house acquired is the house that cracked. Its table of the three plots names the owners: two plots registered to Nechay O., one for individual housing, a garage and dacha construction and one for personal farming, and one to the company LLC Lubny ShBU No.9. It then sets out the case in detail. Oleksiy Nechay, born 1940, retired and living on a pension, owns the plot with the house on it; the house is 60 square metres, built in the 1960s, with a summer kitchen beside it. He gave his grandson Sharay Artem power of attorney on 30 August 2018 to negotiate the price and sale, and the grandson was to buy him accommodation in Poltava and move him there himself, so the addendum records that no further relocation help from the road service was needed. The addendum also says that as of 2 October 2018 the contractor had the owners' written consent "to carry out civil works on their land plots before the payment of compensation", and that no works were being done on the plot holding the house. The counts of affected people do not agree between the two addenda. Addendum No.1 gives 106 in the original 2012 plan rising to 124 as of 30 November 2017, covering 113.8947 hectares and an estimated 70,245,919 hryvnia of compensation. Addendum No.2 gives 121 as of the same date, and 122 as of 31 October 2018, reached by adding two affected people on the Bilotserkivka lot and subtracting one on the Poltava bypass, where a plot found to have three heirs was counted as one after they were paid in equal shares. Neither document explains the difference between 124 and 121. The 2017 addendum also records that the grievance system agreed in the loan agreement was not working: "Establishment of GRM procedures for the project as agreed in the Loan agreement and approved RAP was not fully executed due to various constraints including jurisdictional authority to enforce the same." It says awareness of the mechanism among people in the project area "is very low", that dissemination by the local administration "has been very limited", and that this "has led to an increase in the number of grievances submitted when road construction works commenced". Some people went to the administration or the courts instead. The completion report says the resettlement policy was triggered because the works "required land acquisition causing both physical and economic displacement", that the involuntary resettlement rating was downgraded for periods "due to lack of attentiveness and initiatives on the part of the agencies involved in land acquisition to resolve issues", and that it was later upgraded. The same paragraph says social safeguard compliance "was mainly rated as satisfactory and social impact and risk related to land acquisition and resettlement was assessed as moderate".
bilotserkivka-m03-bypass-house-damage.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 73 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The December 2018 addendum says the design change required one house to be acquired and the involuntary resettlement of one person at Bilotserkivka. bilotserkivka-m03-bypass-house-damage.killed_note: The completion report records deaths at the work sites without counting them: "During project implementation several health and safety related accidents took place in the project construction sites, leading in some of these cases to fatalities." It gives no number, no date and no site, and says reporting of these incidents was inadequate early in the project, so no figure can be entered. The report's only counted death figures are road accident counts: it says fatal accidents on the completed sections fell from 20 a year to a total of 6.
bilotserkivka-m03-bypass-house-damage.outcome: The road and the bypasses were built and the project closed on 30 June 2021. The completion report says the land acquisition problem that mattered most was the delay in government reimbursement, which was resolved when the Bank agreed to finance the acquisitions from the loan. It records no outcome for the damaged house.

muradiye-hepp-urgent-expropriation-van.drop_reason: Cut by the checker, on the lender link and on the tense. First, the link. No document in the set says this loan paid for these plants. The reporting form for the Muradiye plants, the only document in the cache that mentions Muradiye at all, contains no occurrence of "World Bank", "IBRD", "loan", "credit" or "financed": it calls itself a "REPORTING FORM FOR LAND ACQUISITION / SOCIAL IMPACTS OF PORTFOLIO PROJECTS", and the only tie to the project is that it was filed as volume 13 of the RP762 series and that "The Company will update TSKB periodically on land acquisition and resettlement" - a reporting duty to the intermediary, not a statement of which loan paid. The completion report of 19 June 2017 names no sub-project, and the borrower's annex gives only counts by type (12 hydro plants, 4 wind farms, 1 geothermal). The series number is the Bank's disclosure filing, which is nobody's statement about financing. That is round 31's fault 3 and the intermediary precedent on this map, where eleven entries died because the condition sat on the intermediary rather than on the project. Second, the tense, which would decide it even if the link held. The form is dated 12 October 2011 and is written forward: "For Muradiye 976.539 m2 of land will be affected"; "The private land comprises 135 plots and compensation discussions have only recently been initiated"; "the Energy Market Regulatory Authority will file urgent expropriation lawsuits with the local Court of First Instance, with a request for the seizure of the immovable properties listed in the annexed list". The card turned all three into the past ("was affected", "which filed"). The only completed harm the form states is "There are only one masonry house on the land, that is expropriated", one structure and no person, and the parcels marked COMPLETED in its lists, which the form does not attach a loss to. Against that the same document says "There is no grievance until now for the construction of our HEPP project", "no major complaints has been arised", "There are no vulnerable people inhabiting the Project area" and that "local communities are supportive of these developments". Third, what is left. The project-wide statement in the completion report, paragraph 44, is a real admission - "Resettlement in some sub-projects took place without a Resettlement Action Plan (RAP)" - but it identifies no person, no household and no place, and paragraph 43 says the 2,072 people affected across 35 sub-projects "were compensated for loss of assets (including land)", while paragraph 45 records the remedy: the policy framework rewritten in 2011, ex-post social audits of the sub-projects where resettlement happened without a plan, a social development specialist posted in 2012, and additional livelihood measures for some affected people. "Some sub-projects" is thinner than bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears, which names a site and a count of cases, so limb (b) is not met. The Dikili wind farm plan of 1 December 2016 ("The expropriation process is still ongoing and compensations have not been paid yet") is a plan stating an unfinished process, not an outcome. The writer named this its own weakest entry and stated the uncertainty in confidence_note; the uncertainty is the reason for the cut.

dropped_card.community: The completion report of 19 June 2017 says that across the project "35 RE sub-projects (HPPs, wind, solar, and geothermal) led to economic or minor physical resettlement and affected approximately 2,072 people", who, it says, "were compensated for loss of assets (including land)", that a few sub-projects accounted for most of it, and that "Only 6 sub-projects involved physical displacement and affected either one to two houses or other structures like nurseries, gardens and graves." A footnote says gender-disaggregated numbers were recorded in only 11 sub-projects, which affected 410 males and 151 females. The report then records what went wrong. "Resettlement in some sub-projects took place without a Resettlement Action Plan (RAP)." Because the plans were missing, the Bank's team could not identify the shortcomings in them, which the report lists as inadequate grievance mechanisms, "inaccessible consultations due to short notice and location (for example, consultation in village coffee house only with men), inadequate attention to land users without ownership title, and little additional social support for livelihood restoration". The report attributes this to the two lending banks not understanding the policy at first and to the Bank having no social development specialist in the country office. It also records what was done next: the policy framework was rewritten in 2011, the Bank's safeguards team ran after-the-fact social audits of the sub-projects where resettlement had happened without a plan, a social development specialist was posted to the country office in 2012, and the report says the audits led to extra livelihood measures for some affected people. One sub-project's land acquisition is reported in detail. The reporting form for the Muradiye plants, dated 12 October 2011, says 976,539 square metres of land was affected, of which 697,397 square metres in 135 plots was privately owned, and that "The total number of people (number of share holders of real estates) affected from expropriation is 128 and 113 of them are male, 15 of them is female." It says "There are only one masonry house on the land, that is expropriated." The expropriation was decided by the Energy Market Regulatory Board, which filed urgent expropriation lawsuits in the local Court of First Instance "with a request for the seizure of the immovable properties listed in the annexed list and the determination of expropriation fees", so the land could be taken before the price was fixed. The form's three expropriation lists name each owner and village; 151 parcel entries are marked completed and 78 as continuing. The villages are Gumustepe, Yukariargit, Asagiargit, Kandahar, Kemer, Kemerkopru and Gorecek in Muradiye district and Ayranci in Caldiran district. The form says: "Although there are a number of court actions underway related to the directly affected landowners seeking additional compensation monies, TSKB's review indicates that local communities are supportive of these developments and that no community resistance to the construction of these projects has been identified to date." It also says no villages lie in the directly impacted areas, that most of the land is stony with little cultivable ground, and that the company paid for road improvements, school and mosque repairs and new village access routes. At another sub-project the compensation had not been paid when the plan was written: the abbreviated plan for the Dikili wind farm at Kandira, dated 1 December 2016, says 40 per cent of the 8 kilometre transmission line route is privately owned and that "The expropriation process is still ongoing and compensations have not been paid yet", covering 90 square metres to be expropriated and 20,000 square metres of easement.
dropped_card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 65 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document in the set counts people relocated. The completion report says six sub-projects involved physical displacement affecting one to two houses or other structures each, and the Muradiye reporting form records one masonry house expropriated. Those are counts of structures, not of people.

dropped_card.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2016 having disbursed almost twice its original commitment. The borrower's annex says the money financed 12 hydro plants, 4 wind farms and 1 geothermal plant. tuz-golu-gas-storage-informal-households.community: The project built underground gas storage caverns, wells, a surface facility and gas, water and brine pipelines on the Tuz Golu plain. The completion report says the works needed about 749 hectares of land, 382 hectares temporarily and 367 permanently, that 44 per cent of it was public and 56 per cent private, and that it affected 4,061 landowners and 1,036 private plots across 27 settlements, with acquisition starting in October 2007. The borrower's annex puts total compensation paid at 4,521,808.51 lira and records no urgent expropriation and no judicial registration of land. Compensation to landowners ran from the start of 2012 to 2015 and was finished in March 2015. Four households were left out of that process. The completion report says: "However, in December 2016, four households, consisting of 17 individuals, located on two parcels, were notified about physical displacement due to safety concerns. The World Bank learned of the issue in April 2017, during the social baseline studies for the follow-on GSEP. It turned out that these households were informal (for 20-30 years) residents of pastureland, which were not recognized under the Turkish Expropriation Law and therefore excluded from the LAP." It then says: "Upon intervention by the World Bank, to ensure compliance with OP 4.12, this group was satisfactorily compensated by BOTAS in April 2018 and made eligible for priority hiring during construction and operation periods, before having to vacate the land in December 2018." The borrower's annex gives the same facts from its own side: four affected informal households were identified at well site UGS 8, the Bank asked BOTAS for an ex post social audit to make sure their livelihood losses were identified, and after that audit "additional livelihood compensation payments were made by BOTAS to the four households, which consist of 17 persons". The plan completion report of 23 June 2016, written before this came to light, covers only the 64 owners whose land was taken permanently. It says 33 of them "cannot be reached due to living in other cities or residing abroad", so the survey covered the 31 living in the area, that for all 31 the whole parcel was taken because the remainder would not have been usable, and that 18 of them gave farming as their main source of income. Of those surveyed, 19 said the acquisition would affect them positively, 7 said it would have no effect, 2 expected to be affected adversely and 1 was unsure; 16 of those farming the acquired land already had other land. On grievances it says "No specific complaint has been recorded from affected land owners. However, some grievances were received during consultation meetings regarding the remaining part of land after acquisition or damage to lands/crops", which were settled by paying for crop damage. Once the facility was operating the completion report records "a prolonged grievance received from local community members regarding the odor generated from the main facility", for which BOTAS says engineering studies were done and the recommended fix carried out.

balakhani-landfill-families-and-waste-pi.point: The settlement of Balakhani in Baku, as OpenStreetMap records it. The resettlement plan places the landfill next to Boyuk Shor lake and about 3 kilometres from the settlement, and gives no coordinate.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P110679, ARP II Integrated Solid Waste Management Project. Loan 7549-AZ (IBRD-75490, US$29.5 million, agreement conformed 20 May 2009) and additional financing loan 8274-AZ (IBRD-82740, US$47.1 million, agreement 10 January 2014). Approved 17 June 2008, effective 31 July 2009, closed 31 August 2018 against an original closing date of 30 September 2013; US$76.6 million disbursed. The completion report of 28 February 2019 rates the overall outcome Satisfactory and the social safeguards performance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's assessment of 13 September 2021 was a field-based Project Performance Assessment Report.

companies.name: Tamiz Shahar JSC
companies.role: The state joint-stock company that took full ownership and management of the Balakhani landfill on 14 October 2009, ran its rehabilitation, and later operated the materials recovery facility and the waste-to-energy plant. The resettlement plan uses that date as the cut-off for establishing who was affected.

balakhani-landfill-families-and-waste-pi.community: Six families lived on the Balakhani landfill from 1993 to 2009. The resettlement action plan of May 2011 says they have 14 members in total, that they first lived in tents and picked waste, and that they built housing as they earned. It says they bought a shredder in 2004 and built a workshop, bought a second shredder and a washing line in 2006 and built a second workshop, and kept pigs fed on the waste in sheds made from waste materials. The plan says they had no legal claim to the land, which has been designated for landfilling since 1963 and which it describes as severely polluted by municipal, medical and at times hazardous waste. Before the plan was written the residents wrote complaint letters to senior ministers, to government agencies and to the Bank. The plan says: "The letters resulted in an escalation of grievance between all stakeholders in the project and the eventual awarding of a court order to TS JSC supporting the forcible eviction of the PAP. On the insistence of the World Bank and all Government stakeholders the court order was never enacted." It describes the residents' main grievance as a mistaken belief, "borne from miscommunication and misunderstanding", that they would be moved without compensation, and says the plan process had restored harmonious relations. The project also affected people who did not live on the site but earned a living picking waste there. The completion report of 28 February 2019 counts 144 project-affected people in a 2011 survey, including the six families. It says those living on the site were offered apartments in Baku and those whose livelihoods were affected were offered employment, that "Most continued employment either safely at the landfill, or with Tamiz Shahar in the sorting facility with benefits, including pension", that all employees and registered waste pickers were given helmets, gloves and other clothing, and that Tamiz Shahar held 30 individual meetings with waste pickers between September 2014 and February 2015. It notes the project won the Bank's Europe and Central Asia Vice-Presidential Award in 2014, partly for the way the government engaged with the waste pickers. The Independent Evaluation Group's field assessment of 13 September 2021 gives a different count of what happened to them. It says "Six families living at the landfill site were provided with new housing", and then: "However, only 14 of the 100 to 110 waste pickers accepted Tamiz Shahar JSC's proposal and began to work at the facility. Waste pickers reportedly stated that adhering to the eight-hour workday did not suit their preferences." It continues, in a sentence broken by a page break in the report, that currently, as confirmed by the Independent Evaluation Group mission, "only 11 waste pickers from those who were waste picking before the landfill rehabilitation are working at the Balakhani material recovery facility as employees of Tamiz Shahar JSC". It also says some preferred to keep picking at the landfill, that this is allowed under registration and monitoring with safety equipment in place, and that Tamiz Shahar pays waste pickers for plastic, glass and paper collected at the site.
balakhani-landfill-families-and-waste-pi.displaced_label: families who lived on the Balakhani landfill and were provided with new housing, counted by the Independent Evaluation Group's Project Performance Assessment Report of 13 September 2021
balakhani-landfill-families-and-waste-pi.displaced_note: The project's resettlement action plan of May 2011 says the six families have 14 members between them, but that figure is in a plan and no outcome document carries it; the outcome documents count families, not people. The completion report of 28 February 2019 says the six families living by the site "were offered apartments in Baku" and that the government compensated "those living on the Balakhani site with improved housing"; the Evaluation Group's assessment of 13 September 2021 says they "were provided with new housing". ICIJ gives 14 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and happens to equal the plan's count of family members; it is not used here. The project's own counts of affected people are larger and do not agree with each other: the completion report gives 144 project-affected people from a 2011 survey, and the Evaluation Group gives 100 to 110 waste pickers.
balakhani-landfill-families-and-waste-pi.suppression: A court order granting Tamiz Shahar JSC the forcible eviction of the six resident families was issued after they wrote complaint letters to ministers, government agencies and the World Bank. The resettlement action plan of May 2011 says the order was never carried out, on the insistence of the Bank and all government stakeholders.
balakhani-landfill-families-and-waste-pi.killed_note: No death is recorded in the completion report, the resettlement action plan or the Independent Evaluation Group's assessment. The resettlement plan discusses health risks from waste picking, including accidental ingestion, without giving any count of harm.
balakhani-landfill-families-and-waste-pi.outcome: The landfill was rehabilitated into a sanitary landfill with 20 years of capacity and the project closed in August 2018 having spent US$76.6 million. The six families were given new housing. Of the 100 to 110 waste pickers the Evaluation Group counted, 14 took jobs at the materials recovery facility and 11 were still working there when its mission visited in 2021. Picking at the landfill continues under registration.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Project P078933, Education Excellence and Equity Project. IDA credit 41800, XDR 10.50 million committed and XDR 9.83 million disbursed. Approved 1 June 2006, effective 4 October 2006, closed 30 June 2013 against an original closing date of 31 December 2010; restructured 19 March 2010 and 22 March 2012. The restructuring required the recipient to apply the resettlement policy framework retroactively to expropriation already carried out for school construction at Shkodra and other sites, and the amended financing agreement set 30 April 2010 as the date by which the affected party at Shkodra had to be compensated. The completion report of 28 March 2014 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and quality at entry Moderately Unsatisfactory. The European Investment Bank and the Council of Europe Development Bank co-financed the wider programme.

companies.name: Ministry of Education and Science
companies.role: The line ministry that ran the project, wrote the resettlement policy framework and the site plans, carried the expropriation files to the Council of Ministers, and was responsible for paying compensation out of the state budget.

companies.name: Municipality of Shkodra
companies.role: The city government that planned the new school on the site and ordered the demolition of what stood on it.

shkodra-lezha-school-sites-land-cleared.community: The project was not meant to build new schools. The completion report of 28 March 2014 says it became non-compliant with the Bank's resettlement policy in 2008, when it was found that the Bank had approved government investments in new school construction that the financing agreement did not allow. Its safeguards annex says: "Complicating matters, in June 2008, the Municipality of Shkodra ordered demolition of a 5,000 M2 orchard in anticipation of a contract for new school construction. The Municipality alleged that the orchard was public land being used informally by a private individual." The same paragraph says that no new construction had actually begun under the project when the discrepancy was discovered, and the Shkodra site plan says the project did not originally involve the resettlement policy because no new school construction had been contemplated when it was prepared. At the Bank's request the ministry stopped all work on new school construction and agreed to apply the resettlement policy retroactively and take remedial action for the affected party. The site plan of 15 April 2010 gives the detail and a different month. It says that in May 2008 the municipality "demolished the existing improvements on the parcel and removed the agricultural activities being conducted by a local resident". The resident, whose name the plan withholds to protect his privacy, had used the site as a garden for fruit and grapes since the 1990s. The plan says he had built an enclosure of about 4,000 square metres with a concrete-block wall about 2 metres tall and an iron gate, that about 3,600 square metres was planted with grapes and 400 with cherries, that the vines were supported by trellises hung from concrete poles, and that there was a small toolshed on a concrete platform. He used the fruit to make raki and for sale. He went to court in 2008 to establish that the parcel was his; the Shkodra District Court decided in his favour and the Appeals Court overturned that in April 2009, on the ground that his document referred to land in a different neighbourhood. The plan concludes that the state owns the land and he has no legal or legalizable claim, so the policy requires no payment for the land itself, but does require payment for the assets removed, calculated on five years of production and sale of fruit and raki. The amount is withheld from the disclosed version. The plan's own footnotes cut the other way: they estimate he "did not earn more than 5-10% of his annual income from the garden", note that he "still operates a large garden at the site adjacent to his home, a few meters away from the site of the demolished garden", and say the income estimate assumed full retail prices when he consumed or gave away much of the produce. His house was across an alleyway and was not affected, and the plan says he filed no complaint about the amount offered. The completion report says the ministry met the compensation covenant by May 2010. A second site went the same way. The completion report says that in June 2010 the Bank received a complaint that part of the extension of the 9-Year Beslidhja school in Lezha was being built on land restituted to a family, that the Bank asked for all work on that site to stop until the matter was resolved, and that the municipality then decided to expropriate. The ministry's team found that the Hafizi family owned 873 square metres of the land the school stood on. An agreement signed on 1 November 2010 recognised their ownership and allowed the works to resume. The plan of February 2011 values the land at 20,000 lek per square metre, 17,460,000 lek in all, divided between eight named co-owners in shares from one twelfth to one third. The plan says none of the owners lived on the land, had built on it or had cultivated it. The completion report says "ultimately the land owner was fully compensated for the value of the land". A third problem was left unresolved. The completion report says that in 2013 the Bank was told that a small structure next to the Mar Lulaj school in Shkodra, taken to be municipal property due for demolition as part of the school works, was being claimed by a third party. The report says the municipality "closed access to the structure by walling it off to students", that "it was confirmed that the municipality remains in compliance with safeguards policies, although the legal situation of this structure has not yet been clarified", and that if the claim were confirmed the municipality was expected to begin expropriation. It then says: "The contractor, under instructions from the municipality, constructed a wall that prevented access to the structure, and the Bank requested that this be corrected. As of project closing, the current status of this issue was unclear."
shkodra-lezha-school-sites-land-cleared.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 11 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document in the set counts anyone relocated. The Shkodra plan names one affected person and says his house was not touched; the Lezha plan names eight co-owners and says none of them lived on the land.
shkodra-lezha-school-sites-land-cleared.killed_note: No death is recorded in the completion report.
shkodra-lezha-school-sites-land-cleared.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2013. The Shkodra compensation was paid by May 2010 and the Lezha owners were compensated for the value of their land. The completion report says the closing date was extended in part to make up "the 23-months it took to resolve the safeguards issues", and that two of the schools, Mar Lulaj in Shkodra and Keneta in Durres, were still not finished when the project closed. The claim over the walled-off structure beside the Mar Lulaj school was unresolved at closing.

kurgan-tyube-istaravshan-utility-works-a.drop_reason: Cut by the checker. Every loss in this row is assessed, paid and closed in the documents, and no limb of the forward rule is met. Limb (a) fails: no document counts anyone relocated. Limb (b) fails because nothing stayed a harm. The outcome document, the completion report of 25 October 2016, paragraph 39: "There were 21 project affected persons and in each case they received compensation in accordance with the action plans." The borrower's annex to the same report, Table 4, closes each of the five contracts with the same sentence - "The construction contractor compensated the losses incurred according to the Action plan" - including the Farkhor water tank, where it says a residential home's concrete foundation was within the reservoir construction area, damages were assessed at 9,922 somoni, "a different plod of land was given to the owner by the local government of Farkhor" and the contractor paid on top of that. The Istaravshan plan of 2 February 2012 removes the remaining limb (b) candidate, land taken and loss of access: "Tajikistan law does not require any permanent land acquisition for 10 kv line and the farmer may continue to use the land below the line after installation", the loss of access to the 8 metre strip is temporary, each farm has no more than one pole, and the contractor was required to restore the land. The Kurgan-Tyube damage assessment act of 15 December 2010 is signed by the householder himself and prices the fence and the six trees at 14,060 somoni, which the annex says was paid; there is no unpaid balance, no complaint and no claim anywhere in the set. A fence and six trees paid at market value to a man who signed the assessment is not limb (b); it is thinner than bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears, which turns on compensation left unpaid in identified cases. The card also carried a cause the document contradicts: it said the compensation for the Kalai-baland farm rose from 478.08 to 3,087.60 somoni "because 12 trees at two households were to be cut", while the plan gives the reason as arithmetic - "The compensation amount for Kalai-baland Farm was increased from 478.08 TJS to 3087.60 TJS due to a miscalculation in the earlier RAP (0.62 x 4980 = 3087.60)" - and lists the 12 trees as a separate change. The writer named this its own weakest entry.

dropped_card.community: The completion report of 25 October 2016 says: "There were 21 project affected persons and in each case they received compensation in accordance with the action plans." The borrower's annex to the same report lists what was taken, contract by contract, in a table. For the 10 kilovolt overhead line at Istaravshan, a commission found six small farms along the route with a total area given in the table as 3,936 hectares, and damages assessed at 4,980 somoni, reckoned on the market cost of a hectare of irrigated agricultural land. For the line at Vakhdat it found nine small farms with an area of 0.92 hectares and damages of 4,581 somoni. For the line at Kurgan-Tyube it found that trees belonging to four families would be affected and that a fenced wall belonging to a household had to be removed and compensated at market value. For a new 2,000 cubic metre water tank at Farkhor it found that a residential home's concrete foundation was inside the construction area of the reservoir, assessed damages at 9,922 somoni, and records that a different plot of land was given to the owner by the local government of Farkhor as well as compensation from the contractor. For the transmission mains at Farkhor it found a cotton field that had been temporarily occupied, with damages of 4,635 somoni. The annex says the construction contractor paid the losses in each case according to the action plan. One of those cases has its own itemised document. The damage assessment act of 15 December 2010 for the Kurgan-Tyube line was signed by the project unit's chief engineer and chief specialist, the contractor's local engineer, the utility's chief engineer, the chief architect and the householder, named in the act as Tolibov B. It says "the fencing of one of the household which is located along the line should be demolished and its market value shall to be reimbursed", and prices the work: 50 metres of fence dismantled at 900 somoni, earthwork 50, a concrete foundation 3,840, brick lining 6,300, plastering and liming 2,250, and six trees cut at 720, a total of 14,060 somoni. The Istaravshan plan, updated on 2 February 2012, names each affected farm and its compensation: Mamarasul bobo 478.08 somoni, Tuda 1,245.00, Ashurbobo 597.60, Javkandak 4,731.00, Barakat 9,462.00 and Kalai-baland 3,087.60, with full compensation of 21,041.28 somoni. It records two changes from the earlier version: one farm, Pashkent, came off the list because the line was realigned, and the figure for Kalai-baland rose from 478.08 to 3,087.60 somoni because 12 trees at two households were to be cut. The plan says the land itself was not acquired, that the loss of access to a strip 8 metres wide is temporary, that each farm has no more than one pole on its plot, that the farmer may continue to use the land below the line, and that the contractor was required to restore the land to its original condition. It also says representatives of all the farms were present when the land was measured and were shown how compensation was calculated.

itagar-bridge-approach-shed-demolished.drop_reason: Cut by the checker: the harm exists only in a plan written in the future tense, and both outcome documents say the matter closed with the person compensated. The resettlement action plan of May 2014 is prospective throughout - "The shed is subject to demolition as there is no other option of routing the construction area"; "Further, the plot will be used for construction of the bridge approach road for public needs"; "the PAP shall get financial compensation for the cost of labor and materials for recovery of the building" - and the card's own confidence_note concedes that no document states the date the shed came down. A plan saying a thing will be demolished is not actual harm. The outcome documents then close it: the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 31 May 2016 says "one micro-project triggered the involuntary settlement policy. A land acquisition plan was prepared in line with the operational manual, and the affected person was duly compensated", and its field assessment of 16 February 2018 says "There was one instance where a microproject triggered the land acquisition policy, resulting in preparation of a land acquisition plan and compensation to the affected person" and that "no unresolved safeguards issues were reported at project close". The one feature that could have carried limb (b), land taken with nothing paid for the land, is removed by the plan itself: the user had no title, so "The option of land compensation is not considered, as this would not comply with KR land legislation or WB OP 4.12", the plan records that he confirmed the unauthorised use and agreed to the non-compensatory withdrawal at a meeting in April 2014 and signed an act, he was paid 21,194 som for labour and materials under the project's own framework although national law required nothing, and the plan states "The PAP doesn't have any claims to project implementers." Nothing is outstanding.

dropped_card.community: The micro-project rebuilt the Tash-Shoro bridge over the Itagar river, which had been built in 2004 and had lost piers and part of its superstructure, together with a 207 metre approach road. A villager from Itagar had built a livestock shed on the line of the approach, without any land title. The resettlement action plan of May 2014 says the shed "is subject to demolition as there is no other option of routing the construction area" and that it "was constructed informally i.e. without permission to use the plot". The land was taken with no payment for the land. The plan says that is consistent with both Kyrgyz law and the Bank's policy because the user had no title: "withdrawal of the land plot used by the PAP is carried out without land compensation". It records that project representatives, the local government and the affected person met in April 2014, that he confirmed the unauthorised use of the plot and agreed to the non-compensatory withdrawal, and that the participants signed an act for the demolition of the building and the further use of the plot for public needs. Compensation was limited to the cost of labour and materials to rebuild the shed: 21,194 som, itemised as manual excavation, backfilling with pneumatic rammers, a cast-in-situ concrete strip foundation, cob walls, a timber roof framework and corrugated asbestos roofing. The plan notes that Kyrgyz law does not oblige payment to people without title and that this payment exists only because the project's own land acquisition policy framework requires it, and it says "The PAP doesn't have any claims to project implementers." The Independent Evaluation Group's field assessment of 16 February 2018 confirms the outcome and sets it beside a wider land-title problem. It says that during supervision "it was brought to the attention of the World Bank team that six projects had emerged for which there was a lack of clarity around land titles for privately owned land donated to the project or for which planned use of municipal land for microprojects was" restricted by third party use; a page break falls inside that sentence in the report. It then says: "There was one instance where a microproject triggered the land acquisition policy, resulting in preparation of a land acquisition plan and compensation to the affected person." It adds that no unresolved safeguards issues were reported at project close.

bukhara-sewer-pump-station-cleared-plot.community: The resettlement action plan of 18 May 2012, for the contract to rehabilitate existing sewers in Bukhara city, covers a wastewater pumping station of 12 metres by 12 metres, 144 square metres, and the sewer lines running to it. The land it was built on was being used by a householder the plan names as Toychiev Nurjon, of Sitora street number 50, who had no authorised document for it. The plan says the use of the site was granted to the utility by decision number 1067 of 24 August 2010 of the Khokim of Bukhara city, "but unfortunately the nearby householder was informed only verbally about the project". By the time the plan was written the clearing had already happened. It says about 30 metres of the existing fence and the steel entrance gate "have already been dismantled by the contractor with the assistance of the householder worker and stored in the householder stores", and that the brick storage house "was demolished" and its roof, doors and windows and the chicken shelter dismantled and stored the same way. The plot held an old chain-link fence enclosing 1,200 square metres with a steel gate, the fence 88 metres long and 2.5 metres high; a brick store 3.8 by 3.8 by 2.4 metres with a corrugated asbestos roof; a closed steel chicken house; and shrubs, vegetation and trees, for which the plan says there is no accurate count. Because no survey of the planting was done before the works, the compensation was worked backwards from an assumed maximum. The plan says the Bukhara City Beautification Department, as a third party, set the maximum at 21 young plants, and the calculation uses cherry, "the most valuable from the list of fruit trees submitted by the owner": 5 kilograms a year over six years, times 21 trees, times the three years taken for trees to grow back, 1,890 kilograms at 1,200 soums a kilogram, 2,268,000 soums, plus 315,000 soums of labour and gardening costs, 2,583,000 soums for the planting, and a disturbance and inconvenience allowance of 10 per cent on top, 258,300 soums, for a total compensation to the household of 2,841,300 soums. The plan says the store, chicken shelter, fence and gate were to be rebuilt by the utility to a layout agreed with the household, that the contractor was to restore the land, that the household would then be able to cultivate the land around the pumping station, and that the household said no temporary shelter or store was needed while the work went on. An annex to the plan is the household's signed receipt for the cash part of the compensation. The project's resettlement policy framework states that "all compensation and other entitlements will need to be paid prior to proceeding with the civil works", which at this site did not happen. It also says the location of the station was adjusted in consultation with the household to reduce the loss of planting. The completion report of 31 May 2022 says the project had no large-scale resettlement and that most of the works were inside existing facilities or along roads, that four resettlement action plans were prepared and carried out "with adequate compensation paid to project-affected parties by project closing", and then: "However, during implementation, inconsistencies in social safeguard policies were a challenge. For example, there were instances of project-affected persons not being compensated for project impacts on time due to lack of capacity to prepare and implement the Resettlement Action Plans."

georgia-first-east-west-highway-18-plots.drop_reason: No relocation count and no recorded loss. The outcome document, the completion report of 23 December 2013, says at paragraph 2.4.7 that about 23 plots of private land totalling about 3 hectares were expected, that 8 plots were found during implementation to be no longer affected, that three more were added for an underpass and local roads local residents had asked for, and that "Eventually, only 18 land plots were included in the RAP and contracts for compensation were signed with all 18 owners. All compensations were paid to the project affected people. The total amount of compensation was GEL 55,133.85 (about US$ 33,014). No complaints were received." The next paragraph says that on the Rikoti bypass only one permanent structure and some kiosks existed on top of the bypass, "none of which were affected by the civil works" (a footnote marker falls inside that sentence in the report). The project's resettlement policy framework of September 2009 was prepared only in case land had to be acquired for the tunnel works. Checked in the same outcome document: the tunnel collapse during the works, which the report says happened "without fatalities", and the health and safety text, which records no injury. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 30 June 2014 repeats the 18 plots and the payment and adds one observation that does not amount to harm: "There is no direct statement in the ICR that social safeguard policies were satisfactorily complied with." ICIJ gives 52 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. Checked by the checker: paragraphs 2.4.7 and 2.4.8 and the tunnel passage at 2.2.2 read as quoted, and the report's health and safety text records no injury or death at the works. The drop stands.

bulgaria-municipal-infrastructure-dams-p.drop_reason: The land taken during the lender's involvement was paid for before it was taken, and the documents record no loss. The outcome document, the completion report of 22 June 2020, says at paragraph 73: "ALAPs for sub-projects with land related impacts, namely Luda Yana and Plovdivtsi dams, have been fully implemented. No land take occurred without prior compensation. To compensate for the loss of access to grazing land during construction of Luda Yana dam and after impoundment, the Panagyurishte Municipality annually publishes information about available alternative pasture lands on its territory. During Project implementation, no negative livelihood impacts nor physical displacement occurred." Three things were checked before dropping. First, the unpaid balance at Plovdivtsi. The land acquisition plan of June 2014 shows 13 private plots of 0.99 hectares expropriated in December 2012 for 34,923 lev, and a table of 13 families showing 30,288.85 lev, 87 per cent, unclaimed as of 25 September 2013. The same page gives the reason: "The reason for non-payment of the whole amount of compensations is attributed to the lack of filed requests on part of the affected persons to receive the relevant amounts in cash or by way of bank transfer." The money had been transferred to an interest-bearing account at International Asset Bank in December 2012, owners were notified by State Gazette and on municipal notice boards, and the interest is payable to them with the principal. The Luda Yana plan of 27 February 2019 reports the same pattern at that dam: 35 plots and 6.89 hectares expropriated from 35 individuals and one company in 2014 and 2015, with 96.9 per cent of compensation received by August 2018 and the remaining 3.1 per cent held in the district governor's escrow account because owners did not appear. Second, the court case. The only dispute was brought by a company, not by people: "Hydrostroy - P" EOOD appealed the compensation for its land, and judgment 663 of 19 December 2014 of the Pazardjik Administrative Court dismissed its claim for 147,573.01 lev and raised the compensation from 27,750 to 37,660 lev, paid on 19 January 2015. Third, the pre-Bank displacement. The social due diligence of November 2007 for the Neykovtzi dam records that in 1982 the Gabrovo District Municipal Council expropriated yard parcels and buildings in the Kolyo Ganev quarter of Plachkovtsi, that "A total of 4 persons affected have lived in the properties expropriated and the expropriation has resulted in their dsplacement towards other parts of the city of Plachk~ovtzi", and that two of the four were given apartments. That is 1982, 27 years before the loan agreement of 1 February 2010, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 30 October 2020 says "Most of the necessary land acquisition had been completed prior to the Bank's involvement. Past land acquisition was deemed a legacy and not a current issue; OP 4.12 was not triggered." The Neykovtzi dam was dropped from the project in the 2014 restructuring and no land was acquired for it. The plan-reprint check flagged the 0.99 hectare and 13 plot figures. They are not only a plan reprinted: the completion report states them itself at paragraph 72, as land acquired from private individuals in the period 2008-2014, and the Evaluation Group's review attributes them to the completion report's paragraph 71 rather than to the plan. Checked and confirmed by the checker; the figures do not change the drop, because the same paragraph and the next say the land acquired was compensated. ICIJ gives 44 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. Checked by the checker: every quoted sentence above was found in the file named, and the drop stands.

albania-secondary-local-roads-bridge-exp.drop_reason: The forward rule is not met, and the lender-link point the writer led with is overstated. What decides the drop is the outcome document. The completion report of 26 December 2013, paragraph 40, says the issues arising included "a complaint from a resident of Hajmel commune about construction works having a negative effect on a private land, and resettlement and compensation related to the construction of a new bridge in Berat", and that both "were dealt with in accordance with the World Bank policies in a satisfactory manner". It gives no figure for either: no count of affected people, no area, no amount, and no statement of what the Hajmel resident lost. On the bridge it says the 18th century Velabisht bridge was found during work on the local road Ura e Gorices to Fshat Mbreshtan, that it was listed as a Monument of Culture, that it was decided to close it to traffic and build a new bridge nearby, and that the new bridge "required preparation and implementation of site specific EMP and RAP, and expropriation of private land, for which the affected persons were compensated in accordance with the Albanian Law, and satisfactory to the Bank". The Project Performance Assessment Report of 20 December 2018, which is field-based and whose mission visited the site, repeats those two sentences, adds that the new bridge opened to traffic in December 2013 and that the mission confirmed the historic bridge was completed by 2015 and in use, and gives no count and no unpaid balance. Compensated, in accordance with law, satisfactory to the lender, with no count and no stated loss: neither limb of the forward rule is met. On the lender link, the checker reads the documents differently from the writer and the point is not load-bearing. It is true that the borrower's annex says of the replacement bridge "The Works will be financed through OFID funding" and that paragraph 40 says "Works on both bridges are financed by OFID". But the same paragraph calls OFID "parallel co-financing of the SLRP", that is co-financing of this project rather than a separate operation; the bridge came to light "during the improvement of the local road 'Ura e Gorices - Fshat Mbreshtan'", one of the roads this credit paid for; the annex says the Albanian Development Fund "prepared the necessary documentation to comply with the World Bank's Social and Environmental Safeguard policies to enable the land and properties ... to be expropriated"; another bridge contract in the same annex was financed "utilizing money saved from within the Bank/OFID-financed project"; and the assessment report of 2018 does not mention OFID at all when it recounts the episode. The lender link is therefore arguable and the drop does not rest on it. ICIJ gives 3 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people.
